newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Meat trade focus of Australia inspection reform.
newsitem.headline: Meat trade focus of Australia inspection reform.

text.p: Australia's quarantine and inspection procedures, a focal point of its A$2.4 billion annual meat exports, are in for a major shake-up with provisions announced in the Federal budget on Tuesday.
In addition to a A$76 million spending boost over four years to enhance the system, the government will spend A$44.3 million over four years to reform export meat inspection procedures.

New meat inspection measures will help implement a quality assurance system, the Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP), system and will make inspections an industry function, Primary Industries Minister John Anderson said.
Meat inspection reforms would greatly enhance food safety in the meat processing industry while boosting its efficiency and competitiveness, Anderson said in a statement.
Traditional systems for the visual inspection of meat did not fully deal with microscopic agents, he said.

There was now world-wide acceptance that such contaminants were best eliminated by quality control systems such as the HACCP system, which was presently being trialled in five Australian export meatworks under Australian Quarantine and Inspection Service (AQIS) supervision, he said.
A key component of the new system would involve the transfer of responsibility for meat inspection from the government to industry under government supervision and audit, he said.

Results of a trial being conducted in consultation with Australia's overseas meat customers would help ensure international acceptance of integrated quality and inspection systems for the trade in meat and put Australia at the cutting edge of food safety, he said.
The A$44.3 million would be used to reduce the government meat inspection workforce as the role of inspectors was reduced through quality assurance programmes, he said.

As part of the reform package AQIS will be restructured to create a separately-funded and managed meat inspection division. However, the government had decided against creating a separate quarantine and inspection statutory authority with wide-ranging powers, independent of the government, he said.
AQIS would be retained within the Department of Primary Industries and Energy but meat inspection would be established as a stand-alone unit within AQIS, he said.
Australia's import risk analysis process would be upgraded to improve consultation and make it more transparent, while decision-making would remain independent, he said.

Anderson also said that Australia, vitally dependent on export markets and freedom from serious pests and diseases, could not afford to leave its quarantine decision-making processes open to allegations of political interference.
The reforms follow criticism of AQIS by rural and other groups in Australia over disease-control in meat and over the relaxation of imports of products such as cooked chicken meat.
European Union (EU) officials also have recently criticised Australian health inspection requirements, suggesting they are used as non-tariff barriers to block EU rural exports.
